canonical_topic: Seasonal reversal of Pacific Northwest / California power flows
definition: The direction of power flow between the Pacific Northwest, California, and the Desert Southwest changes with the season depending on which region has surplus generation versus peak demand.
core_idea: In spring, snowmelt-driven hydro surplus in the Pacific Northwest flows to higher-demand Northern California; in summer, California imports from both the Northwest and the Desert Southwest to cover peak load; in fall, mild California temperatures combined with continued desert heat can reverse the flow so California exports power to Nevada/Arizona.
key_points: Spring: Pacific Northwest snowmelt produces more hydro power than can be used locally, so it is transmitted mainly to Northern California
Summer: California often imports power from both the Pacific Northwest and the Desert Southwest to meet peak demand
Fall: mild California temperatures versus still-hot Las Vegas/Phoenix can reverse the flow, with California exporting to the desert areas
The direction of flow can change at any time based on the relative temperatures of the regions
trading_implications: Traders need region-by-region temperature/weather forecasts (not just California's) to anticipate the direction of interregional flow and its price impact
Seasonal hydrology forecasts (snowpack) are a leading indicator for spring/summer Northwest-to-California flow volumes
caveats: Power flow direction between these regions is not fixed — it is commonly assumed California is always an importer, but it can become a net exporter to the desert in the fall
